## Proof

Define
$$S(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{|k|}{(1+|x-k|)^{100}}.$$

All summands are non-negative, so $S(x)$ is a well-defined element of $[0,+\infty]$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ (the sum converges for each fixed $x$, since $|k| \le |x| + |x-k|$ gives a summand bounded by $(|x|+|x-k|)/(1+|x-k|)^{100}$, which is summable in $k$ as it decays like $|x-k|^{-99}$).

**Key observation.** Evaluate $S$ at integer points. For any $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, set $x = n$. The summand indexed by $k = n$ is
$$\frac{|n|}{(1+|n-n|)^{100}} = \frac{|n|}{(1+0)^{100}} = |n|.$$

Since every term in the sum is non-negative, we may bound $S(n)$ below by this single term:
$$S(n) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{|k|}{(1+|n-k|)^{100}} \ge \frac{|n|}{(1+|n-n|)^{100}} = |n|.$$

Taking $n \to \infty$ (e.g. $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$), we obtain $S(n) \ge n \to +\infty$. Therefore
$$\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} S(x) \ge \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} S(n) \ge \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} n = +\infty.$$

Hence the supremum is **not finite**; it equals $+\infty$.
